author: Geoffrey A. Moore
introFa: کتاب «Crossing the Chasm: Marketing and Selling Disruptive Products to Mainstream Customers» نوشته Geoffrey A. Moore یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Crossing the Chasm: Marketing and Selling Disruptive Products to Mainstream Customers»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: P1: GOG Aspen Pub./JACM AS101-02 November 5, 2001 18:8 Char Count= 0 Models of Care That Meet the Standards of Crossing the Quality Chasm: A New Health System for the 21st Century Keith D. Moore Dean C. Coddington This article discusses the experience of 11 large health care systems in their attempts to improve quality of care. It focuses on four of the six performance characteristics outlined in Crossing the Quality Chasm, the second report of the Institute of Medicine (IOM): improved effectiveness, renewed focus on patients, timeliness and convenience, and efﬁciency. For example, all of the systems have been making substantial investments in clinical information systems and are beginning to see some of the beneﬁts, including improved quality and coordination of care. Although the Institute of Medicine’s report found that major reform of the U.S. health care system is needed, it is encouraging that a number of organizations are putting forth a signiﬁcant effort toward improving performance and are making progress in the achievement of their improvement goals. Key words: electronic medical records, information technology, patient-centered care The system is failing because it is poorly designed . . . . For too many patients, the health care system is a maze, and many do not receive the services from which they would likely beneﬁt. –William C. Richardson, President, W.K. Kellogg Foundation M ANY OF the recommendations of the second report published by the Insti- tute of Medicine (2001), Crossing the Qual- ity Chasm: A New Health System for the 21st Century, stand in sharp contrast to several current trends in health care. “Back to the basics” is a widely touted strategy for hospi- tals that had previously attempted to take the ﬁrst steps toward becoming integrated health care systems and that suffered ﬁnancially in the process. Single-specialty medical groups are gaining strength in many markets, often at the expense of multispecialty groups. In- vestment in information technology (IT) has been slow to pay off ﬁnancially, and many hospital boards and the leaders of medical groups are questioning the huge sums being spent on further IT development. Imple- mentation of the electronic medical record (EMR) is in its infancy in most parts of the country. In addition, most physicians we have worked with over the years believe that the quality of care they provide to their patients is top quality. Most hospital administrators and board members agree. In fact, we have never worked in a community, no matter how small, where the quality of health care Keith D. Moore, Chairman and CEO, McManis Consulting, Denver, Colorado Dean C. Coddington, Senior Consultant, McManis Consulting, Denver, Colorado The major ﬁndings presented in this article are based on research reported in The Changing Dynamics of Integrated HealthCare:CaseStudiesofMarketLeaders andTheChang- ing Dynamics of Integrated Health Care: Success Factors for the Future, both published by the Medical Group Manage- ment Association. J Ambulatory Care Manage 2002, 25(1), 12–21 c⃝2002 Aspen Publishers, Inc. 12

Copyright 2000. (in the minds of local providers) wasn’t the best in the region! Therefore, incentives to make radical changes of the type advocated in the IOM report are often lacking. “Why do we need to make such changes? We are doing ﬁne and the people in our community appreciate us.” On the other side of the coin, our recent research into 11 large health systems indi- cates high levels of concern over quality of care, meeting patients’ needs, and improv- ing efﬁciency. These systems are investing millions in the development and application of IT, and a substantial portion of the invest- ment has been earmarked for development of an EMR and other clinical initiatives (strate- gies consistent with the IOM report recom- mendations). The 11 health systems studied are identiﬁed in the box. The past experience and the future- oriented initiatives of many of these health systems illustrate various approaches to ac- complishing the six improvement goals cited on pages 41 and 42 of the IOM report. In this article, we focus on four of the six goals: • Effectiveness. Effectiveness is a matter of providing clinical services based on scientiﬁc knowledge and avoiding both underuse and overuse. We include the use of clinical guidelines and other qual- ity improvement initiatives along with increased use of IT. • Patient-centeredness. This includes the growing role of consumers, or patients, in directing (and paying for) their own health care. • Timeliness. Timely care is care provided at the appropriate time. We include con- venience for patients, both convenience scheduling appointments and accessibil- ity. • Efﬁciency. Efﬁciency is equivalent to the avoidance of waste, especially in admin- istrative processes, and the reduction of staff and physician “energy leaks.” EFFECTIVENESS A number of the systems we studied are attempting to increase effectiveness by de- veloping and implementing clinical guide- lines, establishing disease management pro- grams, investing in the clinical aspects of IT, and making sure that their compensation structures do not encourage overuse or un- deruse of clinical resources.

P1: GOG Aspen Pub./JACM AS101-02 November 5, 2001 18:8 Char Count= 0 14 JOURNAL OF AMBULATORY CARE MANAGEMENT/JANUARY 2002 MeritCare MeritCare reorganized itself in 1997, pri- marily to improve the effectiveness of the care it delivers over a region encompassing parts of eastern North Dakota and northwest- ern Minnesota. According to Dr. Roger Gilbertson, CEO, there were a number of problems with the governance and management structure that resulted from the 1993 merger of the Fargo Clinic and St. Luke’s Hospital. “It was cumbersome, and it created silos rather than clinical integration. It did not pro- motepartnershipandaccountabilitybetween physiciansandadministrators.Ibecamecon- vinced of the need for more collabora- tion and standardization across departmental boundaries.” The end result was the creation of a matrix model that includes 10 service lines (or clinical aggregates, as they are called at MeritCare), each headed by a physician and an administrator partnership. Looking back on the reorganization, Dr. Gilbertson said, “We wanted to improve communications, better allocate resources, integrate physicians into accountable roles, speed up the decision-making process, and improve quality of care. There was too much a ‘we and they’ attitude rather than ‘us.”’ These are all part of the IOM deﬁnition of improving effectiveness. One of the results of the new organiza- tional structure has been a 25% reduction in the cost of heart services in just over 2 years. Dr. Gilbertson said, “Furthermore, the quality went up and mortality rates dropped. It was unbelievable.” Dartmouth-Hitchcock Gerald O’Connor, PhD, associate direc- tor of the Center for Evaluative Clinical Sciences (CECS), described an example in bowel surgery: “We cut costs in half and greatly reduced complication rates. Much of this came about by following standing orders. Plus, patient satisfaction went up from 85% to 94%.” The key quality improvement initiatives at Dartmouth-Hitchcock involve micro sys- tems of care. Paul Batalden, MD, a national leader in health care quality improvement, said, “The basic idea is to dig deep into smaller systems to ﬁnd out how processes can be improved.” He estimated that there were at least 200 micro systems of care within the Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center. Mayo Foundation In the years leading up to 1997, there was continuous discussion among Mayo physi- cians about what was known as “The Mayo Model of Care,” but the elements of this model had never been formally deﬁned. The Clinical Practice Committee, one of the most powerful of the 100 committees in the Mayo structure, appointed a work group of 92 physicians to deﬁne the core elements of the Mayo Model of Care. In presenting its recommendations (see box entitled “Core Elements of Mayo’s Model of Care”), the work group noted that there were six conditions that had originally been stated by Dr. William J. Mayo, one of the Mayo brothers, and were still deemed essential to the future success of the Mayo Clinic: 1. continuing pursuit of the ideal of ser- vice and not proﬁt 2. continuing primary and sincere con- cern for the care and welfare of each individual patient 3. continuing interest by every member of the staff in the professional progress of every other member 4. a willingness to change in response to the changing needs of society 5. continuing effort toward excellence in everything that is done 6. continuing conduct of all affairs with absolute integrity

P1: GOG Aspen Pub./JACM AS101-02 November 5, 2001 18:8 Char Count= 0 Crossing the Quality Chasm 15 Core Elements of Mayo’s Model of Care Patient Care • Collegial, cooperative, staff teamwork with multispecialty integration. A team of specialists is available and appropriately used • An unhurried examination with time to listen to the patient • A physician takes personal responsibility for directing patient care over time in a partnership with the local physician • Highest quality patient care provided with compassion and trust • Respect for the patient, family, and the patient’s local physician • Comprehensive evaluation with timely, efﬁcient assessment and treatment • Availability of the most advanced, innovative diagnostic and therapeutic technology and techniques The Mayo Environment • Highest quality staff, mentored in the culture of Mayo and valued for their contributions • Valued professional allied health staff with a strong work ethic, special expertise, and devotion to Mayo • A scholarly environment of research and education • Physician leadership • Integrated medical record with common support services for all outpatients and inpatients • Professional compensation that allows a focus on quality, not quantity • Unique professional dress, decorum, and facilities Source: Reprinted with permission from the Medical Group Management Association Center for Research, 104 Inverness Terrace East, Englewood, Colorado 80112–5306; 303.799.1111. www.mgma.com. Copyright 2000. These six conditions are relevant to achiev- ing improved effectiveness and patient- centeredness as deﬁned by the IOM report. In addition, at the Mayo Clinic there is a strong cultural belief in evidence-based medicine. One physician leader told us, “This is where the real savings in health care will come. There is still tremendous variabil- ity in medicine, and we need to stay after it.” Aurora Health Care Aurora, which serves Milwaukee and much of eastern Wisconsin, has 35 people involved in what Aurora calls care manage- ment, its term for clinical process improve- ment. One of the leaders of this function said, “We strongly believe that there is a need to redesign the delivery of care. Our top man- agement is supportive of clinical improve- ment, and they encourage our efforts.” Aurora had 12 care management initia- tives (compared with 4 in 1996), with task forces working on each one. A staff person told us, “We want consistency, and we want to use a scientiﬁc approach. We are evalu- ating best practices; we go to other orga- nizations and ﬁnd out what they are doing and then apply what appears best to meet the needs of the population we serve.” At Aurora, the trick isn’t in developing the protocols; it is in implementation. Each

P1: GOG Aspen Pub./JACM AS101-02 November 5, 2001 18:8 Char Count= 0 16 JOURNAL OF AMBULATORY CARE MANAGEMENT/JANUARY 2002 initiative also has an outcome measure. As a result of the emphasis on measuring and improving quality, the organization reports major success in its inﬂuenza and inpatient services initiatives. The physician leader of the medical staff of one of Aurora’s hospitals told us that Aurora’s care management initiatives were “tremendous and much appreciated by inde- pendent physicians. The results have been truly amazing. However, we still have a long way to go.” This sentiment would be echoed by physician leaders of all the systems we studied. Combining clinical guidelines and disease management The medical director of Carle Clinic in Urbana said that the clinic had put a substan- tial amount of effort into clinical guidelines: “Nearly every physician has a PC and has ac- cess to guidelines. But we have not done well in terms of implementation.” She went on, “Our experience with guidelines has led us toward further development and implemen- tation of disease management programs.” Carle has undertaken several disease man- agement efforts. For example, the Carle health plan, HAMP, introduced a standard- ized approach to asthma care in 1997, result- ing in the implementation of clinical guide- lines and individual physician feedback. The most comprehensive disease management effort, however, was a diabetes manage- ment program initiated by the joint clinic and hospital organization, Coordinated Care Services. Program components included the standardization of primary physician and nursing care as well as standardized patient education. A 9,000-patient diabetes registry was developed to support the program. Evelyn Quigley, a senior executive at MeritCare, said, “We have moved from the development of clinical guidelines to deﬁn- ing practice guidelines and evaluating clin- ical practice patterns. Guidelines serve as a tool to assist physicians, caregivers, and patients on the ‘how to’ of taking care of chronic illnesses like diabetes and conges- tive heart failure.” Dr. Gilbertson, MeritCare’s CEO, elabo- rated on the growing importance of disease management: “We just inaugurated a dia- betes program. We focus on eye and foot care. Congestive heart failure is another area that lends itself to disease management. A well thought out, standardized approach can reduce hospital admissions from four a year to less than one.” IT and quality of care Here is a summary of four common themes regarding the relationship between IT development and quality of patient care and effectiveness. The EMR The EMR was one of the areas of great- est investment and variation among the or- ganizations we studied. Henry Ford Health System is paperless in the sense that there are no longer paper medical records. Mayo at Jacksonville is also paperless, and Mayo at Scottsdale was scheduled to be paperless in the near future (Rochester continues to rely on paper records). Kaiser Permanente in Colorado, an integrated system of more than 500 physicians, is paperless. The EMRs at Dartmouth-Hitchcock are well along and include 20 data elements. A number of physician leaders and chief information ofﬁcers (CIOs) noted that when voice recognition technology becomes bet- ter developed, it will speed up the process of developing EMRs. One CIO said, “This will greatly reduce physician resistance and make the EMR much more economically feasible.” Linkage with collaborating physicians who are not employed by the health care

P1: GOG Aspen Pub./JACM AS101-02 November 5, 2001 18:8 Char Count= 0 Crossing the Quality Chasm 17 system is a priority for several of the sys- tems we studied. We saw examples of this at Dartmouth-Hitchcock, Aurora, and Moses Cone. Linkage with independent doctors and small medical groups, particularly those that are hospital based, has the potential to be a widespread strategy among large health care systems. Data repositories Clinical data repositories were less well developed than websites, intranets, and EMRs. Henry Ford is the only one of the organizations studied that was fully op- erational with this type of database, al- though others (including Scripps Health in San Diego) were rapidly moving in this direction. Clinical guidelines and disease management Use of the Internet and websites should facilitate disease management programs for patients of many health care systems. For example, the Internet greatly expands the ability of regional health systems to com- municate with patients who have chronic ill- nesses, and use of the Internet for this pur- pose is common among proprietary disease management companies. Intranets Nine of the 11 organizations studied had an intranet (all had Internet websites). Com- mon applications included posting clinical guidelines, clinical and administrative per- formance measures (often referred to as dashboards), job descriptions, clinic board meeting notes, and other information of value to physicians and employees. In some cases, access to the organization’s intranet would allow patients to view their medi- cal records, make appointments, and eval- uate the care they received. (Security and conﬁdentiality issues relating to posting this type of information electronically have been dealt with in these organizations). Patient and provider access to this type of clinical in- formation is consistent with the recommen- dations of the IOM. In the future, we anticipate a substan- tial expansion of intranet use, both in the numbers of systems having an intranet and in the amount of information posted. An intranet can facilitate communications, re- duce the number of phone calls, and con- tribute to the development of a meaningful corporate culture. Overuse and underuse of health care resources The fee-for-service payment system pro- vides ﬁnancial incentives for overuse of health system resources. Capitated payment provides the opposite incentives and is of- ten accused of promoting the underuse of resources. However, capitation is declining in importance, and fee-for-service payment, albeit discounted, is once again becoming almost universal, even in some of the most advanced managed care marketplaces in the country. Even though most of the systems we stud- ied derive the majority of their revenues from fee-for-service payment (or all, in the case of Mayo),severalhavephysiciancompensation arrangements that are not overly depended on productivity (seeing patients; perform- ingprocedures).Someoftheseorganizations consider other factors, such as patient sat- isfaction, measures of quality, contributions to the organization, and leadership in educa- tion and research, in determining physician compensation. With these broader ﬁnancial incentives in place, we believe there is less emphasis on generating revenues and earn- ings by doing too much. However, these are small steps relating to one of the most important public policy

P1: GOG Aspen Pub./JACM AS101-02 November 5, 2001 18:8 Char Count= 0 18 JOURNAL OF AMBULATORY CARE MANAGEMENT/JANUARY 2002 questions facing the country: with the fail- ure of capitation and the move back to fee- for-service medicine, how will health care utilization costs be controlled? Reports of rapidly escalating health care costs are com- ing in every day, but the solution so far has largely been ﬁnger pointing by health plans, employers, consumers, and providers. In our view, “a new health system for the 21st cen- tury” (the subtitle of the IOM report) must come to grips with payment system reform. PATIENT-CENTERED CARE The desire by consumers to have a greater role in their own health care and that of their families is a strongly documented trend that will play out with increasing strength in the next 10 years. We have identiﬁed a number of reasons for the growing role of consumers, and these are summarized in the box entitled “Indicators of More Assertive Consumers.” Most of the major systems included in our research are focusing on patients and better meeting their needs. The emphasis on health plans as customers has diminished. None of the hospital-based systems we studied refer to physicians as their number one customers. Indicators of More Assertive Consumers • Consumers exhibit insatiable appetite for information. ⇒Forty-three percent of Internet users seek health care information. • Complementary and alternative medicine grows. ⇒Money spent on CAM over $50 billion in 2000. • Discretionary health care spending explodes (e.g., cosmetic surgery, high-speed heart imaging, vision correction surgery). • Direct-to-consumer marketing takes off (e.g., pharmaceuticals). • Self-care on the rise. • International consumers seek out services in the U.S. • Choice reigns supreme. Rather, physicians and hospitals view them- selves as partners in meeting the needs of patients. These are important attitude shifts that should beneﬁt consumers and make care more patient centered. The Mayo Model of Care (summarized earlier in the box entitled “Core Elements of Mayo’s Model of Care”) is based on a comprehensive list of what consumers want from health care providers. Two of the items, italicized in the box, emphasize meeting the needs of patients. The culture of Mayo goes backtothebeliefsandactionsofitsfounders. Dr. Will Mayo, one of the Mayo brothers, said, “The best interest of the patient is the only interest to be considered.” Although many physician leaders today might state it differently, all of the leaders of the sys- tems we studied expressed a renewed com- mitment to meeting patient needs. TIMELINESS The timeliness of care is an especially crit- ical problem in inner city and rural areas. One of the systems we studied, MeritCare, is making a special effort to speed up the delivery of care to residents of its generally rural service area.

Open access In an effort to reduce the waiting time from the ﬁrst call for an appointment to the time the patient sees a health care provider (physician’s assistant or physician), Merit- Care has developed a system of open ac- cess that allows patients in rural areas to see providers on the same day they call for an ap- pointment. A physician leader of MeritCare told us, “This is a higher level of customer services that we have to offer if we are go- ing to be competitive. Our tests show that it works; it is more efﬁcient for both physicians and patients. It cuts administrative costs as- sociated with making and changing appoint- ments and calling people to conﬁrm that they are coming in.” Geographic coverage and convenience One of the hallmarks of the health sys- tems studied is the taking of health services to the patients where they live and work. All of the systems have regional networks of pri- mary care ofﬁces and smaller clinics offer- ing some specialty services (and one system, Aurora, has a network of close to 100 retail pharmacies). Consumers, especially seniors, love the convenience of these types of net- works. Figure 1 shows MeritCare’s regional net- work. We include this as an example typical of the large health care systems we studied. These kinds of networks, combined with ef- forts like those of MeritCare, represent a big step forward in meeting the IOM report’s call for timeliness—and convenience—in the de- livery of care. EFFICIENCY According to various sources, the amount of waste in health care ranges from 25% to as much as 40% of all health care dollars. This includes the overuse of resources dis- cussed earlier as well as the high amounts of spending on administration (estimated by various sources as representing one-quarter of all health care spending). Of course, these “wasted” dollars represent revenues and earnings for many hospitals, medical

P1: GOG Aspen Pub./JACM AS101-02 November 5, 2001 18:8 Char Count= 0 20 JOURNAL OF AMBULATORY CARE MANAGEMENT/JANUARY 2002 groups, and suppliers of goods and services to the health care industry. What can be done to cut down on the amount of “waste” in health care? The health systems studied don’t have the complete answer, but several are making an effort to reduce their clinical costs and ad- ministrative expenses, as indicated by the following examples. Park Nicollet Health Services Park Nicollet, formerly known as Health- System Minnesota, ﬁnds that it has no choice buttoimproveitsefﬁciencythroughITbased automation. The CIO told us, “We have a fundamental goal to be digital. We are in a race against time. The labor market doesn’t allow us to increase stafﬁng to handle calls. We have trouble hiring and retaining clerical staff.” He went on, “Each of our clinics re- ceives 500 to 1,100 phone calls a day. With e-mail, this could be reduced. But this de- pends on a secure environment.” The CIO said that “it costs an average of $3 to $10 to handle each telephone call ver- sus pennies for e-mail. We have 45 million calls a year at Park Nicollet, and 5.5 million arefrompatients.Halfamillionofthesecalls are abandoned. The rest are calls we make among ourselves.” The CIO explained the dilemma this way: “As a $500 million organization, we aren’t big enough to develop the IT systems we need. We can’t get where we need to go incrementally. Therefore, we need a private ﬁrm with capital as a partner.” Park Nicollet is moving in this direction. Carle Clinic Carle, based in Urbana, Illinois, has a spe- cial reason to be concerned about efﬁciency: about half the patients it serves are members of its health plan. Although provider-owned health plans have generally fallen out of favor, several systems (e.g., Scott & White, Marshﬁeld Clinic in Wisconsin) continue to own these plans, and they are an important part of the systems in terms of generating patients, dollars, and incentives to improve efﬁciency. Improving efﬁciency: An overview All of the systems we studied were concerned about improving efﬁciency (and their ﬁnancial performance) through per- formance improvement—automating wher- ever possible (as described by the CIO at Park Nicollet), reducing stafﬁng, improving scheduling and the use of human resources, redesigning administrative and clinical pro- cedures, and questioning the value versus costs of all departments. CONCLUSION The purpose of this article is to show how several large systems are moving ahead in four important areas: improved effective- ness, a renewed focus on patients, timeliness and convenience, and efﬁciency. We believe that hospitals, independent physicians, and smaller medical groups have similar oppor- tunities to address the performance improve- ment areas cited in the IOM report. Although we did not discuss safety and equity, the two remaining performance char- acteristics,the11systemswestudiedarealso making progress on these fronts. Quality of care as it relates to patient safety is obviously a high priority among the large systems we studied. Their investment in IT is one part of addressing the issue of patient safety (e.g., more accessible medical records, few drug errors). Equity, in particular, making med- ical services available regardless of ability to pay, is also a major concern, and the sys- tems included in our study provide millions of dollars a year in charity care. Of course, the same thing could be said about most hospitals, physicians, and medical groups.

P1: GOG Aspen Pub./JACM AS101-02 November 5, 2001 18:8 Char Count= 0 Crossing the Quality Chasm 21 The provision of health care to the uninsured or those who do not pay for one reason or an- other continues to be an under appreciated contribution of the health care system as a whole. Although reforming the U.S. health care system in the manner suggested by the IOM report appears, on the surface, to be a daunt- ing task, the fact that a number of orga- nizations are making signiﬁcant efforts to improve their performance is encouraging. While none of the health systems studied would claim to have all the answers, they are moving forward with initiatives that are consistent with the recommendations of the IOM report. REFERENCE Institute of Medicine. (2001). Crossing the quality chasm: A new health system for the 21st century [Report by the Committee on Quality of Health Care in America]. Washington, DC: National Academy Press.
